intro.young: Bone looks solid, but up close it is full of tiny tubes and living cells!
intro.junior: Compact bone is built from many osteons: tiny tubes of hard bone arranged in rings around a central canal. Inside is lighter spongy bone filled with marrow.

text.young: Hard bone is made of rings stacked like the rings of a tree trunk.
text.junior: Each osteon is a cylinder of concentric bone layers called lamellae. Thousands of osteons packed together make compact bone strong.

text.young: A tiny tube in the middle carries blood, so the bone gets food and oxygen.
text.junior: The central canal of each osteon carries blood vessels and nerves along the bone.

text.young: Living bone cells sit in little gaps between the rings and look after the bone.
text.junior: Osteocytes live in small spaces called lacunae and keep the bone healthy. Tiny channels connect them so they can share nutrients.

text.young: Inside, bone has a light, holey pattern like a sponge. It's strong but not heavy.
text.junior: Spongy bone is a lattice of thin struts called trabeculae. It keeps bones light while still spreading the load.

text.young: Soft marrow inside your bones makes new blood cells every day.
text.junior: Red bone marrow fills the spaces of spongy bone and produces red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets.

intro.young: A muscle is made of lots of long, thin threads bundled together, like a rope.
intro.junior: Skeletal muscle is made of long cells called muscle fibres, grouped into bundles called fascicles. Stripes (striations) show the tiny contracting units inside.

text.young: Each thread is a long muscle cell that can get shorter to pull.
text.junior: A muscle fibre is a single long cell that can be several centimetres long. It shortens (contracts) when a nerve signal arrives.

text.young: Threads are wrapped together into bundles, and bundles make a whole muscle.
text.junior: Fibres are grouped into fascicles, each wrapped in connective tissue called the perimysium.

text.young: The stripes are tiny parts that slide together to make the muscle shorter.
text.junior: The light and dark bands are rows of sarcomeres, where actin and myosin filaments slide past each other during contraction.

text.young: Each muscle thread has lots of control centres along its edge.
text.junior: Skeletal muscle fibres have many nuclei, pushed to the edge of the cell.

text.young: Tiny blood tubes bring oxygen so the muscle has energy to work.
text.junior: Capillaries run between the fibres, delivering oxygen and glucose and taking away carbon dioxide.

intro.young: Nerves are made of special cells called neurons that pass messages along, like runners in a relay race.
intro.junior: Nervous tissue is made of neurons, which carry electrical signals, and supporting glial cells. Signals pass from one neuron to the next at synapses.

text.young: The cell body is the neuron's control centre.
text.junior: The cell body contains the nucleus and keeps the neuron alive.

text.young: Little branches catch messages from other neurons.
text.junior: Dendrites are branching extensions that receive signals from other neurons.

text.young: The long tail carries the message away, very fast.
text.junior: The axon carries the electrical signal (nerve impulse) away from the cell body, sometimes for more than a metre.

text.young: A fatty coat wraps the tail, like plastic around a wire, to make messages go faster.
text.junior: The myelin sheath insulates the axon. Signals jump between the gaps (nodes of Ranvier), which makes them much faster.

text.young: At the end, the message is passed to the next cell.
text.junior: Axon terminals release chemical messengers called neurotransmitters across a tiny gap, the synapse, to the next cell.

intro.young: Your skin has layers, like a sandwich, and each layer has a job.
intro.junior: Skin has three main layers: the epidermis on top, the dermis with glands, hair follicles and nerves, and the fatty hypodermis underneath.

text.young: The thin top layer keeps germs and water out.
text.junior: The epidermis is a thin, waterproof layer of cells that are constantly replaced from below. It contains melanin, which gives skin its colour.

text.young: The thick middle layer is strong and stretchy.
text.junior: The dermis contains collagen and elastic fibres, blood vessels, nerves, hair follicles and glands.

text.young: A soft fat layer keeps you warm and cushions bumps.
text.junior: The hypodermis stores fat, which insulates the body and absorbs shocks.

text.young: Each hair grows from a tiny pocket in your skin.
text.junior: A hair follicle is a pocket in the dermis where a hair grows. A tiny muscle can pull the hair upright, giving you goosebumps.

text.young: Sweat glands make sweat to cool you down when you are hot.
text.junior: Coiled sweat glands release sweat through pores. As it evaporates, it cools the body.

text.young: Tiny blood tubes bring food and oxygen to your skin.
text.junior: Blood vessels in the dermis widen to lose heat when you are hot and narrow to save heat when you are cold.

text.young: Touch sensors tell your brain when something touches you.
text.junior: Sensory receptors in the skin detect touch, pressure, vibration, heat, cold and pain, and send signals along nerves to the brain.
